places.tradition: Position fixed by narrative function alone (Leaf 1912); no mound at Hisarlık is matched to it
places.note: The barrow of 'ancient Ilus son of Dardanus,' out on the plain: Hector holds council beside it, away from the din (10.415); the routed Trojans stream past it (11.166); Paris shoots Diomedes from behind its grave-stele (11.371-372); and Priam's wagon passes it on the way to beg for Hector's body (24.349). Strabo (13.1.36-37) already treats the plain's tombs as an identification problem, not a solved one.

sources.cite: Leaf, Walter. Troy: A Study in Homeric Geography. London: Macmillan, 1912.
Rose, C. Brian, and Reyhan Körpe. "The Tumuli of Troy and the Troad." In Tumulus as Sema, edited by Olivier Henry and Ute Kelp. Berlin: De Gruyter, 2016.

places.name: The barrow of old Aesyetes
places.tradition: Position fixed by function alone — high enough to see the camp, close enough to run home (Leaf 1912); no mound identified
places.note: The Trojans' own watch-post: Polites sits on its summit, 'trusting in his swiftness of foot, waiting for when the Achaeans should set out from the ships' (2.793-794).

sources.cite: Leaf, Walter. Troy: A Study in Homeric Geography. London: Macmillan, 1912.

places.name: The confluence of Simoeis and Scamander
places.tradition: Position shifts with the delta's six-millennia progradation (Kraft, Rapp, Kayan, and Luce 2003); no fixed Bronze Age location recoverable
places.note: 'Where the Simoeis and Scamander join their streams' (5.774) — Hera unyokes her horses here, and Simoeis makes ambrosia grow for them, a real divine landmark inside the poem.

sources.cite: Kraft, John C., George Rapp, İlhan Kayan, and John V. Luce. "Harbor areas at ancient Troy: Sedimentology and geomorphology complement Homer's Iliad." Geology 31, no. 2 (2003): 163–66.

places.name: The ford of the fair-flowing river
places.tradition: Position unrecoverable; the delta has prograded past it (Luce 1998)
places.note: A fixed crossing, named by a repeated formula: 'but when they came to the ford of the fair-flowing river, eddying Xanthus, whom immortal Zeus begot' (14.433 = 21.1-2 = 24.692-693). It marks the seam between camp-side and city-side of the plain, and Achilles splits the rout there (21.3).

sources.cite: Luce, J. V. Celebrating Homer's Landscapes: Troy and Ithaca Revisited. New Haven: Yale University Press, 1998.

places.name: The Scamandrian plain
places.note: The battlefield itself: the Achaeans 'poured out onto the Scamandrian plain' and 'took their stand in the flowery Scamandrian meadow' (2.465-467). Kraft, Kayan, and Erol's geomorphology puts the usable Late Bronze Age plain south and west of Hisarlık — the reverse of the ground north of the site that most illustrations still use.

sources.cite: Kraft, John C., İlhan Kayan, and Oğuz Erol. "Geomorphic Reconstructions in the Environs of Ancient Troy." Science 209, no. 4458 (1980): 776–82.

places.name: The Bay of Troy (the silted embayment)
places.note: Not named by Homer, but the single most important thing to get right on the map. A marine embayment once reached roughly 10 km south of Hisarlık at maximum Holocene transgression (Kraft, Kayan, and Erol 1980); the ria intruded some 17 km up the lower Karamenderes valley by 7000–6000 BP (Kayan); progradation had carried the coast west of Troia by c. 4000 BP; and a 2–2.5 m Late Bronze Age sea-level fall left a shallow lagoon behind a wide sandy barrier, with swamp over much of the delta. The modern coast lies about 6 km north of the site.

sources.cite: Kraft, John C., İlhan Kayan, and Oğuz Erol. "Geomorphic Reconstructions in the Environs of Ancient Troy." Science 209, no. 4458 (1980): 776–82.
Kraft, John C., George Rapp, İlhan Kayan, and John V. Luce. "Harbor areas at ancient Troy: Sedimentology and geomorphology complement Homer's Iliad." Geology 31, no. 2 (2003): 163–66.

Kayan, İlhan. "Geoarchaeological Interpretations of the 'Troian Bay.'" In Troia and the Troad: Scientific Approaches, edited by Günther A. Wagner, Ernst Pernicka, and Hans-Peter Uerpmann. Berlin: Springer, 2003.

places.name: The Achaean camp and ships
places.tradition: Position fixed by the poem's own spatial logic (14.31-36), not by any excavated trace
places.note: The poem is exact about the camp's shape even where it will not fix its ground: the ships were drawn up in rows because the beach, wide as it was, could not hold them all, and they 'filled the whole long mouth of the shore, as much as the headlands enclosed' (14.31-36) — a beach between two headlands. The traditional headlands are Sigeion and Rhoiteion; Beşik Bay is the archaeological alternative.

sources.cite: Kraft, John C., George Rapp, İlhan Kayan, and John V. Luce. "Harbor areas at ancient Troy: Sedimentology and geomorphology complement Homer's Iliad." Geology 31, no. 2 (2003): 163–66.
Luce, J. V. Celebrating Homer's Landscapes: Troy and Ithaca Revisited. New Haven: Yale University Press, 1998.

places.name: The Achaean wall and ditch
places.tradition: Erased inside the poem itself — Poseidon and Apollo turn the eight Idaean rivers against it after the war (12.17-24); Aristotle already noted this as the poet's own device (ap. Strabo 13.1.36)
places.note: Built in a single day round the pyre-barrow: a wall with high towers and chariot-wide gates, and beyond it a deep, wide ditch set with stakes (7.436-441). The poem provides for its own disappearance, which is exactly why nothing of it has ever been found.

sources.cite: Strabo. Geography 13.1.36.
Hainsworth, Bryan. The Iliad: A Commentary, Volume III: Books 9–12. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1993.

places.name: The assembly and law-place, with the gods' altars
places.tradition: Position fixed by the poem's own spatial logic (11.806-808), not by any excavated trace
places.note: Located precisely within the camp: 'when he came running to the ships of godlike Odysseus, where their place of assembly and of justice was, and where the altars of the gods had been built for them' (11.806-808) — read together with 8.222-226, this puts the camp's civic centre exactly at its midpoint.

sources.cite: Luce, J. V. Celebrating Homer's Landscapes: Troy and Ithaca Revisited. New Haven: Yale University Press, 1998.

places.name: The ship and hut of Odysseus
places.tradition: Position fixed by the poem's own spatial logic (8.222-223 = 11.5-6), not by any excavated trace
places.note: At the exact middle of the line of ships: Agamemnon and Strife both stand on its deck 'to shout to either side' (8.222-223 = 11.5-6) — the camp's midpoint, and its civic centre.

sources.cite: Homer. The Iliad. Translated by A. T. Murray. Loeb Classical Library 170–171. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1924.

places.name: The huts of Ajax son of Telamon
places.tradition: Position fixed by the poem's own spatial logic (8.224-226 = 11.7-9), not by any excavated trace
places.note: One extremity of the camp: he and Achilles 'had drawn up their balanced ships at the ends, trusting in their manhood and the strength of their hands' (8.225-226 = 11.8-9). Which end is Ajax's and which Achilles' the poem never says.

sources.cite: Homer. The Iliad. Translated by A. T. Murray. Loeb Classical Library 170–171. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1924.

places.name: The hut of Achilles
places.tradition: Position fixed by the poem's own spatial logic (8.225-226 = 11.8-9), not by any excavated trace
places.note: The camp's other extremity, opposite Ajax — the setting of the Embassy in Book 9 and of Priam's supplication in Book 24. Its distance from the centre is a plot device: Achilles cannot see what is happening at the ships and has to send Patroclus to find out (11.599ff.).

sources.cite: Homer. The Iliad. Translated by A. T. Murray. Loeb Classical Library 170–171. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1924.

places.name: The hut of Agamemnon
places.tradition: Position fixed only by implication — near the centre — not by any excavated trace; named directly at several points across the poem (2.9, 9.178, 9.669, 19.241, 23.38)
places.note: The command tent, named directly and often: Zeus sends the destructive Dream 'to the hut of Agamemnon son of Atreus' to open Book 2 (2.9); the envoys of the embassy set out from it (9.178) and report their failure there on return (9.669); Agamemnon's reconciliation gifts are fetched from it (19.241); and the army gathers there after Patroclus's death (23.38). Homer never fixes it in the line of ships; it sits near the centre only by implication.

sources.cite: Homer. The Iliad. Translated by A. T. Murray. Loeb Classical Library 170–171. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1924.

places.name: The barrow of Achilles and Patroclus
places.tradition: Discussed among the Troad's hero-tumuli by Rose and Körpe (2016), who find the surviving 'tomb of Achilles' candidates to be later cult sites, not burials
places.note: Achilles orders a modest barrow for Patroclus now, to be made 'broad and high' later by whichever Achaeans outlive him (23.245-248). The Odyssey delivers the sequel: their bones mixed in one urn, Antilochus's set apart, under 'a great and faultless barrow on a jutting headland by the broad Hellespont, so as to be visible far off from the sea to men now alive and those to come' (Od. 24.80-84).

sources.cite: Rose, C. Brian, and Reyhan Körpe. "The Tumuli of Troy and the Troad." In Tumulus as Sema, edited by Olivier Henry and Ute Kelp. Berlin: De Gruyter, 2016.

places.name: The tomb of Hector
places.tradition: No location given in the poem, and none claimed for it in antiquity — unlike the other Trojan War tombs, it never became a cult site in the Troad
places.note: The last image of the poem: the bones laid in a hollow grave, covered with great close-set stones, the barrow heaped in haste with lookouts posted all round against an Achaean attack (24.797-801).

sources.cite: Homer. The Iliad. Translated by A. T. Murray. Loeb Classical Library 170–171. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1924.

places.name: Kesik Tepe (the 'Demetrius tumulus'), claimed tomb of Achilles
places.tradition: Fourth-century BC and later hero-cult identification with Achilles' tomb (Arrian, Anabasis 1.12)
places.note: The most impressive mound on the Trojan plain, close to ancient Sigeion. By the 4th century BC it was regarded as Achilles' tomb, and Arrian reports Alexander sacrificing to Achilles on landing near Sigeion. The coordinate is from Vici.org and has not been checked against a published survey plan.

sources.cite: Livius.org, s.v. "Troy 5."
Vici.org, s.v. "Kesik Tepe."
Rose, C. Brian, and Reyhan Körpe. "The Tumuli of Troy and the Troad." In Tumulus as Sema, edited by Olivier Henry and Ute Kelp. Berlin: De Gruyter, 2016.

places.name: Beşik-Sivritepe (Achilleion), claimed tomb of Achilles
places.tradition: Hellenistic hero cult of Achilles at the Achilleion sanctuary, Beşik-Yassıtepe
places.note: A Hellenistic tumulus roughly 2 km SSW of Yeniköy at the north end of Beşik Bay, associated with the Achilleion sanctuary — a rival 'tomb of Achilles' to Kesik Tepe, which is itself the evidence that these are competing cult claims, not burials.

sources.cite: Vici.org, s.v. "Beşik-Sivritepe."
Rose, C. Brian, and Reyhan Körpe. "The Tumuli of Troy and the Troad." In Tumulus as Sema, edited by Olivier Henry and Ute Kelp. Berlin: De Gruyter, 2016.

places.name: Kum Tepe
places.tradition: Schliemann's identification with Achilles' tomb, the Achilleum of the ancient sources
places.note: A mound near the Hellespont entrance that Schliemann took for the tomb of Achilles. Rose and Körpe's survey work shows it is in fact a Neolithic-to-Bronze-Age settlement mound, not a tumulus at all — one of several such reclassifications in the Troad.

sources.cite: Vici.org, s.v. "Kum Tepe."
Rose, C. Brian, and Reyhan Körpe. "The Tumuli of Troy and the Troad." In Tumulus as Sema, edited by Olivier Henry and Ute Kelp. Berlin: De Gruyter, 2016.

places.name: The tomb of Ajax at İn Tepe (Aianteion)
places.tradition: Ancient hero cult of Ajax at Rhoiteion; Pliny, Natural History 5.125; Strabo 13.1.30
places.note: A conical mound on a spur of the Rhoiteion promontory, west of İntepe village; Pliny says a town was built beside Ajax's tomb, and the tumulus was rebuilt and vaulted in the 2nd century AD. Coordinate left null: the Vici.org record places it at Kumkale, roughly 8 km west of İntepe, almost certainly in error. Anchor conceptually to Rhoiteion (40.010, 26.303) until a published survey point is found.

sources.cite: Pleiades. "Rhoiteion." Place 550856.
Rose, C. Brian. The Archaeology of Greek and Roman Troy. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2014.

places.name: Üvecik Tepe
places.note: South of Troy on the road to Alexandria Troas — and not a heroic tomb at all. It is the tomb of Festus, a favourite of Caracalla, himself a great admirer of Achilles; built c. 214 AD, it became the largest tumulus in the Troad. A clean illustration of how the Homeric landscape kept being manufactured under Rome.

sources.cite: Pleiades. "Uvecik Tepe." Place 897256486.
Livius.org, s.v. "Troy 5."
Rose, C. Brian. The Archaeology of Greek and Roman Troy. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2014.

places.name: Sigeion
places.note: Not named in the Iliad. A later Greek settlement at the mouth of the Scamander, forming the northwest corner of the Troad and the traditional western headland of the Achaean beach.

sources.cite: Pleiades. "Sigeion." Place 550877.
Cook, J. M. The Troad: An Archaeological and Topographical Study. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1973.

places.name: Rhoiteion
places.note: Not named in the Iliad. An Archaic-to-Hellenistic city on the Baba Kale spur of Çakal Tepe, its Aeantion promontory serving as a harbour in Roman times — the traditional eastern headland of the Achaean beach, paired with Sigeion.

sources.cite: Pleiades. "Rhoiteion." Place 550856.
Cook, J. M. The Troad: An Archaeological and Topographical Study. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1973.

places.name: Adramyttium
places.note: Not named in the Iliad. An Aeolian city on the Karataş peninsula at Ören, Balıkesir province, included here because Strabo measures Homeric Thebe from it (60 stadia) — the anchor for a whole cluster of southern-Troad identifications.

sources.cite: Pleiades. "Adramyttium." Place 550403.
Strabo. Geography 13.1.61–65.

places.name: Beşik Bay
places.note: A bay on the Aegean coast southwest of Troy, facing Tenedos. Korfmann's 1982-87 excavation found a cemetery of roughly 100 graves here in which Mycenaean and Mycenaeanising LH IIIB fine ware runs to about a third of the wares — against under 1% at Troia VI/VII itself — making it the strongest archaeological candidate for a working Late Bronze Age port. Coordinate left null; anchor from Beşik Tepe at the bay's north end, 39.9171 / 26.1591.

sources.cite: Korfmann, Manfred. Beşik-Tepe excavation reports, 1982–1987.
Kraft, John C., George Rapp, İlhan Kayan, and John V. Luce. "Harbor areas at ancient Troy: Sedimentology and geomorphology complement Homer's Iliad." Geology 31, no. 2 (2003): 163–66.

places.name: The Kesik basin / Kesik cut
places.tradition: Eberhard Zangger's port hypothesis, with Jablonka and Kayan on the associated water-engineering system — contested, sedimentation ambiguous and diagnostic artefacts absent
places.note: An artificial cut through the 40 m Yeniköy ridge west of the plain, and a former marsh, drained in the 1960s, shown by drilling to have been a marine basin in the Early Bronze Age. Zangger proposed a rectangular basin roughly 330 x 230 m functioning as a naval station or trans-shipment point; the case is thin and should be presented as a hypothesis only.

sources.cite: Zangger, Eberhard. "Searching for the Ports of Troy." Academia.edu.
Jablonka, Peter, and İlhan Kayan. "Artificial Ports and Water Engineering at Troy: A Geoarchaeological Working Hypothesis." ResearchGate.

places.name: Gargaron, the topmost peak of Ida
places.tradition: Identification with the summit of Mount Ida / Kaz Dağı, following Strabo 13.1.5
places.note: Zeus's own seat: 'Gargaron, where he has his precinct and his fragrant altar' (8.48); Hera comes to 'topmost Gargaron' (14.292) to win him over there, and he sleeps and wakes there (14.352, 15.152). Not to be confused with the historical coastal town of Gargara below it.

sources.cite: Cook, J. M. The Troad: An Archaeological and Topographical Study. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1973.
Strabo. Geography 13.1.

places.name: Cape Lekton
places.note: Modern Cape Baba, the westernmost point of Asia Minor. Named once: Hera and Sleep 'came to Lekton, where first they left the sea' and went on over dry land to Ida (14.284) — one of Homer's very few precisely verifiable coordinates.

places.name: The heaped-up wall of Heracles
places.note: The pro-Greek gods' vantage point for the battle of the gods: 'the high heaped-up wall of divine Heracles, which the Trojans and Pallas Athena had made for him, so that he might escape the sea-monster when it drove him from the shore to the plain' (20.145-148) — Callicolone's opposite number across the divine grandstand.

sources.cite: Homer. The Iliad. Translated by A. T. Murray. Loeb Classical Library 170–171. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1924.

places.name: The Satnioeis river
places.tradition: Identification with the Tuzla Çayı, following Strabo 13.1.50
places.note: 'The banks of fair-flowing Satnioeis' (6.34); Satnios is born there to a nymph and a herdsman (14.445), and 'steep Pedasus' stands on it (21.87).

sources.cite: Cook, J. M. The Troad: An Archaeological and Topographical Study. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1973.

places.name: The Aesepus river
places.note: Modern Gönen Çayı, the eastern limit of Trojan-allied territory: Pandarus's Zeleians 'drink the dark water of Aesepus' (2.825), and it is one of the eight Idaean rivers Poseidon and Apollo turn against the Achaean wall (12.21). Pleiades records it as a line, not a point, and so does this gazetteer. See also 'aesepus', a duplicate record kept for a single catalogue reference.

places.name: The Granicus river
places.tradition: Identification with the Biga Çayı, standard since antiquity
places.note: One of the eight Idaean rivers of 12.19-22 — later famous as the site of Alexander's first victory in Asia. Rose and Körpe surveyed the lower Granicus valley's tombs.

sources.cite: Rose, C. Brian. The Archaeology of Greek and Roman Troy. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2014.

places.name: The Rhodius river
places.tradition: No secure modern identification; variously placed east of the Scamander since antiquity (Leaf 1923)
places.note: One of the eight Idaean rivers, named once (12.20) and nowhere else in Homer.

sources.cite: Leaf, Walter. Strabo on the Troad: Book XIII, Cap. I. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1923.

places.name: The Rhesus, Heptaporus, and Caresus rivers
places.tradition: Already puzzling to ancient geographers; none securely identified with a modern watercourse (Leaf 1923)
places.note: Three more of the eight Idaean rivers, named in a single line (12.20) and nowhere else — honestly listed as unlocated Idaean streams, not guessed at.

sources.cite: Leaf, Walter. Strabo on the Troad: Book XIII, Cap. I. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1923.

places.name: The Thymbrios river
places.tradition: Strabo 13.1.35
places.note: Not named by Homer. A Scamander tributary identified with the Kemer Su, included as the anchor for locating Thymbra at their confluence.

sources.cite: Strabo. Geography 13.1.35.

places.name: The hut and ship of Nestor
places.tradition: Position not fixed by the poem's one passage that places Achilles, Ajax and Odysseus in the line of ships (8.222-226 = 11.5-9) — Nestor's ship is not named there — and no excavated trace exists; Patroclus reaches it at a run from Achilles's station at one end of the line (11.617), which puts it somewhere short of that end, but no more precise position is ever given.
places.note: Nestor's ship and hut, reached three times at moments that turn the plot. Agamemnon convenes the council of elders that hears the destructive Dream ‘beside the ship of the Pylos-born king’ (2.53-54 = Νεστορέῃ παρὰ νηῒ Πυλοιγενέος βασιλῆος). On the night of the Doloneia, unable to sleep, Agamemnon goes to rouse Nestor for a second council and ‘finds him beside his hut and black ship’ (10.73-74). And in the poem's own hinge, the wounded Machaon is driven there from the field; Achilles, watching from his own ship, sends Patroclus running the length of the camp to ask after him (11.599-618) — the errand that puts Patroclus in front of Nestor's long appeal on his return, the appeal that sets the rest of the poem in motion.

sources.cite: Homer. The Iliad. Translated by A. T. Murray. Loeb Classical Library 170–171. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1924.

places.name: The Trojan bivouac on the plain
places.tradition: Position fixed only by the poem's own relative description — ‘between the ships and the streams of the Xanthus’ (8.560) — not by any excavated trace or an absolute site.
places.note: The Trojans' one recorded night in the open. On Hector's order, flushed with the day's success, they camp on the plain beside the ships instead of withdrawing into Troy, ‘between the ships and the streams of the Xanthus’ (8.560). A thousand fires burn there, fifty men waiting by the light of each blaze for dawn and battle (8.562-563) — the image the poem holds a moment, comparing the fires to stars around a bright moon on a windless night (8.555-559), before returning to the horses standing in harness, watching for the throned Dawn (8.564-565).

sources.cite: Homer. The Iliad. Translated by A. T. Murray. Loeb Classical Library 170–171. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1924.

places.name: The camp of Rhesus and the Thracians
places.tradition: Position fixed only by the poem's own relative description — the newest-arrived of Troy's allies, camped apart, outermost of all (10.434) — not by any excavated trace or an absolute site.
places.note: The camp of Rhesus, king of the Thracians: newest come to Troy and posted apart from the rest, ‘outermost of all’ (10.434) — the position the captured Dolon gives away under interrogation, along with a boast about Rhesus's gold-and-silver chariot and horses whiter than snow (10.435-441). Odysseus and Diomedes go straight there: Diomedes kills Rhesus and twelve sleeping Thracians while Odysseus drags the bodies clear so the panicked horses will not shy at them, and the two drive the horses back to the ships (10.469-514).

sources.cite: Homer. The Iliad. Translated by A. T. Murray. Loeb Classical Library 170–171. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1924.

places.name: The pyre of Patroclus
places.tradition: Position fixed only by the poem's own spatial logic — piled on ‘the headland’ where Achilles had already marked out ground for the barrow (23.125-126) — not by any excavated trace.
places.note: Where Achilles burns Patroclus. Wood cut on Ida is piled ‘on the headland, where Achilles had marked out a great mound for Patroclus and for himself’ (23.125-126); the pyre itself — named outright, ‘the pyre of Patroclus’ (23.192, πυρὴ Πατρόκλου) — is built a hundred feet square, loaded with sheep and cattle, jars of honey and oil, four horses, two of Patroclus's own dogs, and twelve captured Trojan youths, and burns through the night on winds Achilles prays down from Boreas and Zephyrus (23.163-225). At dawn the bones are gathered into a golden urn and Achilles orders a barrow raised over them — but only a modest one for now: ‘not very large, but such as fits; afterward let the Achaeans make it broad and high, whoever of you are left in the benched ships when I am gone’ (23.245-248). That later, far larger monument, shared in the end with Achilles's own bones, is the Odyssey's sequel and is catalogued separately as tomb-of-achilles-and-patroclus; this record is the pyre and the first, modest barrow Book 23 itself completes (23.255-257).

sources.cite: Homer. The Iliad. Translated by A. T. Murray. Loeb Classical Library 170–171. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1924.

places.name: The ground of Patroclus's funeral games
places.tradition: Position fixed only by the poem's own spatial logic — the same ground as the pyre and barrow (23.257-258), with the chariot course running out into the level plain (23.358-359) — not by any excavated trace.
places.note: Immediately after the barrow is closed, Achilles holds the people ‘right there’ (αὐτοῦ) and seats them in ‘a wide gathering-place’ for the games (23.257-258, εὐρὺν ἀγῶνα) — the same ground as the pyre and barrow, not a separate site; the poem gives it no other bearings, and calls the gathering itself an ἀγών again when it breaks up at the start of Book 24 (24.1, Λῦτο δ' ἀγών). Only the chariot race reaches beyond it: Achilles sets the turning-post ‘far off, in the level plain’ (23.358-359), a landmark Nestor describes only as either an old gatepost or ‘the grave-mound of some man dead long ago’ (23.331) — Homer leaves the marker's identity undetermined, and so does this record.

sources.cite: Homer. The Iliad. Translated by A. T. Murray. Loeb Classical Library 170–171. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1924.
